Post text:
Almost two in five people with dementia in England still have no recorded diagnosis.

That is not because families failed to notice. It is because a change in thinking is still treated as something that can wait.

Without a diagnosis there is no care plan, no honest conversation about driving or money, and no alert on the hospital record.

If you have been told it is just old age, and the person you love is not who they were a year ago, ask the GP for a cognitive assessment and a history from someone who knows them.

Delay is not neutral.
Caption: Underdiagnosis is a system pattern, not a family failure.
Source: Lang et al. BMJ Open 2017 PMID 28159845; Dementia Commission 2023 ~36% undiagnosed in England.

Post text:
A meta-analysis of 23 studies found that about 62% of people living with dementia were undetected.

The rate was higher in the community than in care homes, and higher still in some low-income settings.

Undetected dementia is how people arrive in hospital with no baseline and a note that says query confusion, query baseline.

A diagnosis is not a sentence. It is the information the rest of the system needs to stop guessing.
Source: Lang L et al. BMJ Open 2017;7:e011146. PMID 28159845. Pooled undetected dementia 61.7%.

Post text:
English primary-care research found that the median time from meeting dementia criteria to a recorded diagnosis was about three years.

Three years of families rearranging a life around a problem official systems have not named.

While you wait for a clinic letter you can still document a baseline: what they cooked last Christmas, whether bills are being paid, whether familiar routes are still safe.

The administrative diagnosis can lag. The practical one should not.
Source: Aldus CF et al. Undiagnosed dementia in primary care. NIHR 2020. Median time to diagnosis ~3 years.

Post text:
When people say dementia they usually mean Alzheimer's.

NHS figures suggest dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia affect far more people than the recorded diagnoses.

Fluctuating attention, early falls, vivid visual hallucinations, or a change in personality and tact are not difficult behaviour. They are clues to the subtype.

If that is the picture, ask whether Lewy body disease or a frontotemporal syndrome has been considered. Do not accept dementia as a finished sentence.
Caption: Alzheimer's is not the only dementia. It is the one we remember to look for.
Source: NHS primary care dementia figures 2024 on DLB/FTD gap.

Post text:
We diagnose the dementias that present as a memory-clinic memory problem.

We miss the ones that present as apathy, language change, poor judgement, or she is just not coping.

If your only trigger for referral is a low MMSE, you will miss people whose memory is relatively spared.

Ask about work, money, cooking, routes and social tact. Those are cognitive tests. They do not require a booklet.
Source: Aldus et al. 2020: diagnosis likelier with memory/orientation impairment than other deficits.

Post text:
Before anyone concludes that your parent has dementia, ask two unglamorous questions.

When were the hearing aids last worn?
When were the eyes last tested?

The Lancet Commission keeps hearing impairment on the prevention list for a reason. Untreated hearing loss drives isolation that looks like withdrawal, and it is associated with faster cognitive decline.

A hearing test is not a memory clinic. Sometimes it is why a memory clinic can wait.
Source: Livingston G et al. 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia. PMID 39096952.

Post text:
A ten-minute conversation with the patient alone is not a dementia assessment.

People with emerging dementia can still manage a social exchange in a consulting room. That is why we take a history from someone who has seen the last six months at home.

If you are the daughter in the waiting room, say so: I need to tell you what a normal Tuesday looks like.

That sentence prevents a lot of false reassurance.

She is not herself is a medical presentation. It is not a diagnosis.

Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, depression, side-effects of tablets, and delirium all still masquerade as dementia. Some of them are treatable. All of them deserve bloods and a timeline before anyone writes advanced dementia on a referral.

I have seen profound hypothyroidism referred as irreversible decline. The man returned when we treated the thyroid.

Ask what reversible causes have been checked. It is a reasonable question.
Caption: Ask what has been ruled out, not only what has been named.

Post text:
Dementia diagnosis rates in England improved for years and then slipped after the pandemic.

The target has been that two-thirds of expected cases should have a recorded diagnosis. Large parts of the country have not held that line.

A missed diagnosis is not only a clinic statistic. It is an older person on a ward with no alert, no care plan, and a family who have been told there is nothing to name.

Ask your local practice what their diagnosis rate is. It is published. It should be uncomfortable if it is low.
Source: NHS England primary care dementia data; Future Health 2024.

Post text:
People living alone are less likely to receive a dementia diagnosis than people living with a spouse.

That is not a biological finding. It is what happens when the system relies on someone else to raise the alarm.

If your parent lives alone and the neighbours have started to mention the bins, the post, or the cooker, that is collateral history. Write it down. Take it to the GP.

Living alone is a risk factor for being missed, not a reason to wait.
Source: Aldus et al. 2020: living with a spouse increased odds of diagnosis (OR 2.38).

Post text:
Young-onset dementia is underdiagnosed in part because we do not expect it.

Depression, marital strain, work failure and alcohol are the labels that get used first. Sometimes they are also true. They do not exclude a cognitive disorder.

If a 58-year-old is losing the ability to organise a working day, take a history that includes language, behaviour and navigation, not only mood.

Age is a prior. It is not a veto.
Source: NICE NG97 young-onset; BMC Geriatr 2024 capture-recapture.

Post text:
More than one in three people with dementia in the UK remain undiagnosed. Of those who are diagnosed, many still have no care plan.

A diagnosis without a plan is an unfinished sentence.

Ask, after the letter arrives: who reviews this, what happens if things change, and who do I call when the next crisis starts at 22:00.

The clinic appointment is not the intervention. What follows it is.
Caption: A diagnosis without a care plan is an unfinished sentence.

Post text:
South Asian older adults in English analyses have been less likely to have dementia identified than White peers.

That is not a footnote. It is a group of families being told later, in a language that may not be theirs, after a crisis rather than before one.

If you work in a practice that serves that community, a low diagnosis rate is not a reassuringly healthy population. It is a case-finding problem.

Use the family. Use the language the family uses.
Source: BMC Geriatr 2024 capture-recapture: lower identification in South Asian group.

Post text:
If the GP says come back in six months, ask what you should watch for in the six months.

Getting lost on a well-known route. Mixing up tablets. Not managing a bill that used to be routine. A personality that has hardened or flattened.

Those observations are data. Bring them written down.

Watchful waiting without a watch list is just waiting.

An MMSE of 26 does not close the case if the daughter describes a year of lost cooking, lost money and lost routes.

Bedside tests have floors and ceilings. Collateral history does not.

If the test and the family disagree, believe that there is a problem and keep looking. Do not use a near-normal score as a discharge from thinking.
Source: NICE NG97: do not rule out dementia on a single cognitive test.

Post text:
Driving is often the argument that forces a diagnosis into the open.

It is also the argument that families postpone because they do not want to be the person who took the keys.

You do not have to win that argument alone. You can ask the clinician to put fitness to drive in writing and to notify the process that your country uses.

Safety is not disloyalty. It is one of the reasons diagnosis exists.
Caption: Safety is not disloyalty. It is one of the reasons diagnosis exists.

Post text:
Hospitals still admit older people with obvious long-standing cognitive decline and no recorded diagnosis.

Then we argue about baseline on a Sunday night with a locum and a thin set of notes.

Case-finding in hospital is not theft of the memory clinic's job. It is how we stop pretending we do not know.

If the 4AT attention items fail and the family describe a two-year story, write suspected dementia as well as delirium.

You are allowed to ask for a second opinion.

A rushed reassurance that everyone forgets names is not a second opinion.

If two separate people who know your parent well are worried, and one consultation was not, the worry is still information.

Take a written timeline. Take a medication list. Take a sibling. The quality of the assessment often rises with the quality of what you bring.

Depression in later life and early dementia overlap. Treating one does not forbid assessing the other.

A six-week trial of an antidepressant is not a cognitive assessment.

If function is sliding while mood lifts only a little, keep the dementia question open. Do not let the first label use up all the curiosity.

By 2040 the UK is projected to have well over a million people with dementia. If diagnosis rates stay where they are, hundreds of thousands will still be unnamed.

That is not an abstract curve. It is future families standing in the same GP corridor having the same argument.

The personal version of the policy problem is: ask for the assessment now, while there is still a person who can tell you what they want from the years ahead.
Caption: Ask for the assessment while they can still tell you what they want.
Source: Future Health 2024 projection of undiagnosed cases by 2040.

Post text:
Underdiagnosis is worse when the first language of the home is not the language of the clinic.

Cognitive tests designed in English, delivered through a rushed interpreter, will undercall and overcall.

Use an interpreter. Use a family member for collateral, not as a translator of the test.

A wrong test in the wrong language is not better than no test. It is a false number with a letterhead.

If your parent is in a care home and nobody has ever explained the diagnosis, ask for a review.

People move into care with a label of frailty or after a fall, and the cognitive diagnosis is assumed rather than made.

Assumed dementia leads to assumed nothing-to-be-done. Made dementia can still lead to hearing aids, pain treatment, a medication review and a plan for when they are frightened.

Do not use age as a reason not to diagnose.

A 91-year-old with a two-year story of lost function still benefits from a named diagnosis: medication review, hearing, pain, legal planning, and a family who stop blaming themselves.

The phrase she is 91 is an observation. It is not a cognitive assessment.
Source: NICE NG97 applies across later life.

Post text:
The first person to worry is often right.

In study after study, informants notice change before a short clinic test does.

If you are that person, you do not need a medical degree to say: something is different, here are six examples, please take this seriously.

That is how underdiagnosis ends in one household, even when it has not ended in the country.
Caption: The first person to worry is often right.

Post text:
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not publish diagnosis rates as cleanly as England. That should not comfort anyone.

Where measurement is weak, underdiagnosis is easier to ignore.

If you work in those systems, ask your board what number they trust and what they are doing to it. If they have no number, that is the number.

A normal CT scan does not mean there is no dementia.

CT is for looking at other things: bleed, tumour, large stroke, significant hydrocephalus. Many people with Alzheimer's have a CT that a busy report calls age-related change.

The diagnosis lives in the history and the examination of thinking. Imaging supports. It does not veto.

Write the suspected diagnosis in the discharge letter even if the memory clinic has not confirmed it.

Primary care cannot code what you never mention. The next admitting team cannot protect what they cannot see.

Suspected dementia, collateral from daughter, 4AT 4 on admission, recovered to 1, please refer — that is a useful paragraph.

Silence is how underdiagnosis reproduces itself between sectors.

If new treatments for early Alzheimer's arrive in your health system, they will only reach people who already have a diagnosis.

That is the unromantic reason to push on case-finding. Not because a drug is a miracle. Because eligibility starts with a name on a record.

Even if no drug is right for your parent, the name still opens therapy, social care and planning.

Underdiagnosis blocks all of it.
Caption: New treatments only reach people who already have a name on a record.

Post text:
A family told me: he was sharp on Monday. By Wednesday he did not know my name.

That is not how dementia behaves.

Dementia changes over months and years. A change over hours or days is delirium until proven otherwise.

Something medical is happening now. Ask the staff when the change started. If the answer is this week, do not let the notes say progression of dementia unchallenged.
Source: Wilson JE et al. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020 PMID 33184265.

Post text:
Delirium and dementia travel together. That does not make them the same illness.

Dementia is the vulnerability. Delirium is the acute brain failure on top.

If there is already a dementia diagnosis, the risk of delirium in hospital is high. That is why a new change still needs a work-up.

She has dementia is the start of the assessment, not the end of it.
Source: Marcantonio ER. N Engl J Med 2017 PMID 29020579.

Post text:
If you are at a hospital bedside and the person you love is new, strange, frightened or vacant, say this out loud:

Has anyone formally assessed for delirium?

You are naming the condition that affects about one in four older people in hospital and is still written down as confused, query baseline.

Write down their normal Monday. Staff cannot detect a change they have not been told about.
Source: Gibb / Siddiqi Age Ageing 2020 PMID 32043137. Occurrence ~23%.

Post text:
I have seen progression of dementia written when the collateral history was two days long.

Two days is not progression. Two days is an acute event.

The next step is not a dementia referral. The next step is the trigger that started on Tuesday: infection, new drug, pain, retention, constipation, low oxygen, low sodium, a fall nobody saw.

Time course first. Labels second.
Caption: Speed of onset is the most underused diagnostic test in medicine.

Post text:
You cannot properly assess for delirium when someone already has dementia is a sentence I still hear.

It is wrong.

The 4AT was designed to be usable in that exact situation. A recent meta-analysis in dementia populations reported sensitivity around 88% and specificity around 79% across more than a thousand patients.

Dementia makes assessment harder. It does not make assessment optional.
Source: Tieges Z et al. Age Ageing 2021 4AT accuracy PMID 33951145; Keane 2026 dementia subgroup.

Post text:
Delirium is common. About one in four older medical inpatients. The published occurrence has barely moved in four decades.

What has also barely moved is public vocabulary. Families know the word dementia. They do not know the word for the sudden version.

If you take one thing from this account, take the word. Use it at the bedside. Ask for it by name.
Source: Age Ageing 2020 PMID 32043137; Int J Nurs Stud 2025 pooled prevalence 23.6%.

Post text:
A chart review study found roughly nine times more in-hospital delirium than discharge codes admitted.

Staff often describe the confusion in the notes. The diagnosis still never lands on the letter.

That is how a treatable brain failure becomes a vanished event. No code, no audit, no follow-up, no family explanation.

If you saw delirium, write the word. Not only the adjective confused.
Source: Age Ageing 2024;53:afae006 PMID 38364815. Chart review vs discharge codes.

Post text:
Your loved one's new confusion is not just old age.

It is almost certainly delirium: a medical condition, often treatable, always deserving of a cause.

Ask the staff about it. If there is no diagnosis, make sure they know about the change from last week, and ask specifically about delirium.

Old age is a category. It is not a mechanism.
Caption: Old age is a category. It is not a mechanism.

Post text:
Delirium disables its own witness. The organ affected is the one the patient needs in order to report the problem.

That is why we look for it, rather than waiting to be told.

Every older person coming in unwell deserves a proactive check of attention and awareness. Not when they are noisy. When they arrive.

Delirium after an emergency admission is associated with later dementia, including in people who did not already have a heavy burden of long-term conditions.

That finding is inconvenient for any story of dementia as only a slow protein disease.

It is also a prevention opportunity: detect the delirium, treat the causes, reduce the insults, follow the brain afterwards.

If your service discharges delirium without a cognitive plan, you are leaving the second half of the illness on the table.
Source: Davis DHJ et al. Brain 2012 PMID 22879644; Penfold et al. Lancet Healthy Longevity 2026.

Post text:
Do not promise yourself a fixed recovery date after delirium.

Some people are much better in days. Some remain changed for weeks. A minority stay different.

Ask for an honest range, and ask what change should trigger review.

The question is not when will he be himself. The question is how will we know if this is still delirium, still a cause, or a new baseline that needs a different plan.

A brain that changed overnight deserves the same urgency as a heart that did.

We have pathways for chest pain. We still treat an acute change in attention as furniture.

The difference is not evidence. It is habit.

Write delirium on the list of problems. Give it a cause search. Review it tomorrow. That is the whole protocol, and we still skip it.
Caption: A brain that changed overnight deserves the same urgency as a heart that did.

Post text:
The noisiest patients get the most attention. The quiet ones may be sicker.

Hypoactive delirium is the withdrawn, barely-eating, staring-at-the-ceiling form. It does not generate incident forms. It generates the word settled.

Settled is not a mental state. It is often an unexamined one.

If an older person has gone quiet in hospital, that is a reason to assess for delirium.
Source: Krewulak et al. Crit Care Med 2018 PMID 30234649.

Post text:
Hyperactive delirium gets treated because it is inconvenient. Hypoactive delirium gets missed because it is convenient.

The prognosis runs the other way.

A 4AT on the patient who is no bother is how you find the person the ward has stopped seeing.
Source: Avelino-Silva et al. hypoactive mortality PMID 25482070.

Post text:
If the ward says she is settled, ask what that means.

Is she eating. Is she speaking in sentences. Does she know where she is. Can she keep her attention on you.

Settled can mean peaceful. It can also mean hypoactive delirium.

You are allowed to ask for a proper check of her thinking, not a reassurance that she is not causing trouble.

Mrs P was 83. Quiet. Eyes on the ceiling. Lunch untouched. Not pressing the bell.

In a busy ward, quiet patients become settled patients.

A student sat down. She thought she was at home. She had pneumonia and constipation already being treated, and no formal recognition that the quietness was delirium.

Hypoactive delirium is commoner than the shouting kind. It carries a worse prognosis. It is detected less because it does not disrupt the ward.
Caption: Quiet is not the same as well.

Post text:
If the nursing comments say confused query baseline for two days and nobody has done a structured test, that is not a baseline problem.

That is an assessment problem.

Baseline is established by collateral history. Delirium is established by examining attention now.

Do both. Do not let query baseline become the whole diagnosis.

People with hypoactive delirium often look depressed.

They may also be depressed. The two are not alternatives.

A vacant older person who became vacant this week needs a delirium work-up first. Antidepressants can wait a week. The infection, the retention and the missed fracture cannot.

Delirium treatment should involve brain care and mind care. The latter is often missing.

Even a quiet patient can be frightened. They may not have the words.

Sit down. Say where they are and why. Do not test orientation as a sport. Offer one true sentence and stay long enough for it to land.

Orientation should be gentle.

Say where the person is and why, then offer reassurance rather than testing them repeatedly.

Repeating what day is it to a frightened person is not therapy. It is an exam they keep failing in public.
Caption: Orientation should be gentle, not an exam.

Post text:
Agitation is not a personality.

In a care-home cluster trial, a stepped pain-treatment protocol reduced agitation in people with dementia.

That should have ended the habit of reaching for a sedative before anyone has looked at the mouth, the bladder, the skin, the hips and the bowels.

If the notes already say behavioural, the next line should be an examination.
Source: Husebo BS et al. BMJ 2011;343:d4065. PMID 21765148.

Post text:
Mr T, 88, with dementia, became aggressive at night. Sedation was already written up.

A nurse saw him wince when rolled. An unwitnessed fall had left an impacted hip fracture. He had been walking on it.

Regular analgesia changed the nights. No antipsychotic was required.

In dementia, pain rarely arrives as a sentence. It arrives as fight, or as silence.

Before you write BPSD, write a list.

Mouth. Ears. Constipation. Retention. Fracture. Wound. Skin. Hunger. Fear. Need for the toilet.

I do not know a shorter way to reduce inappropriate antipsychotic use on a geriatric ward.

The abbreviation is not a diagnosis. It is a postponement of thinking.

If your parent with dementia has become distressed during washing, ask whether anyone has examined them properly.

A bruise on a hip, a urine-soaked pad left too long, a sore mouth, a hidden pressure area: these are common, and they do not announce themselves.

You can say: I think this is pain. Please look before you sedate.

That is not interference. That is information.
Caption: Say: I think this is pain. Please look before you sedate.

Post text:
The agitation was pain. It very often is, especially after surgery.

When someone is agitated and delirious, the first question is not what do we give them. It is what is causing this.

Pain. Infection. Retention. Constipation. Hypoxia.

Treat those, and a surprising number of nights settle without an antipsychotic.

PAINAD takes a minute. It watches breathing, vocalisation, face, body and consolability.

It is imperfect. It is better than guessing.

If you work with people who cannot give a pain score out of ten, use an observational scale rather than interpreting the shout as a psychiatric event.
Source: Warden V et al. PAINAD 2003 PMID 12711742.

Post text:
Night-time shouting after a new admission is not a reason to write the person off as a sundowner.

Sundowning is a description of clock time. It is not a diagnosis of cause.

Ask what hurts at night. Ask whether the pad is wet. Ask whether they can see the toilet. Ask whether the last dose of pain relief was at tea-time.

The clock is a clue. It is not the disease.

People with dementia still feel pain. What they lose is the ability to locate it, time it, and bargain about it.

That is why a grimace during rolling is data, and a denial of pain in a sunny moment is not a veto.

Believe the body.
Caption: Believe the body.

Post text:
An antipsychotic written up as if required for personal care is often a failed pain plan.

Look at the last 24 hours of analgesia before you look at the mental health act paperwork.

If paracetamol has been omitted and opioid has been timid, fix that first.

After a fall that nobody saw, do not accept she is just more confused as the whole story.

Unwitnessed falls hide fractures. Impacted hips can still walk, after a fashion.

If rolling, dressing or standing now causes a fight that was not there last month, ask for a good look at the bones, not only the behaviour.

Constipation is an undignified cause of a dignified person's distress.

It is also common, detectable, and treatable.

If the last recorded bowel motion is not on the chart, that is a finding. If the abdomen is loaded, that is a finding.

Not every crisis is a scan. Some of them are a bowel chart.

Urinary retention can present as distress, agitation or worsening confusion.

It does not always present as I cannot pass urine.

If your parent is writhing, standing, tugging at clothes, or newly delirious, ask whether a bladder has been checked.

A scanner takes seconds. A missed retention can take a person apart.
Caption: A bladder scanner takes seconds. A missed retention can take a person apart.

Post text:
Resistance to care is often fear of the unannounced.

Hands arriving without warning feel like an assault to a person who does not know the room.

Warn, ask, explain. I am going to check your pulse, is that all right.

Most so-called resistance falls when the body is given a second of prediction.

They told me I had been a bit confused. That is not what it was like.

For the patient, delirium can be terror and a certainty of harm. Hearing it called a bit confused waves the worst hours of their life away.

Ask first what it was like. Listen. Then match your language to their reality.

If your parent is frightened in hospital, your face is treatment.

Not a metaphor. Familiar faces reduce distress in people with delirium and dementia.

Sit where they can see you. Say who you are. Say you will stay for a bit.

The medicine still matters. So does the person who makes the room make sense.
Source: Hshieh TT et al. JAMA Intern Med 2015 PMID 25643002.

Post text:
A fall in an older person is not an accident with furniture. It is a medical event until you have asked why.

Was there a faint. A trip. A new tablet. A rush to the toilet. A drop in blood pressure on standing.

The family question is simple: has anyone done a falls assessment, or have we just picked her up.
Caption: A fall is a diagnosis that has not been made yet.

Post text:
Exercise that challenges balance reduces falls in older people living at home.

Cochrane reviews put the reduction in fall rate at around a quarter for balance and functional programmes.

A leaflet that says be careful is not an intervention.

If your parent has fallen and the only plan is try not to do it again, the plan is incomplete.
Source: Sherrington C et al. Cochrane 2019 PMID 30703272.

Post text:
Families often tell me about the third fall.

The first two were nothing. No faint. No injury. So nobody looked at standing blood pressure, vision, bone health, or the sleeping tablet started in February.

Most hip fractures are preceded by a career of uncounted near-misses.

After one fall to the floor, ask for an assessment. After two, insist.
Source: NICE NG249; World Falls Guidelines 2022 PMID 36178003.

Post text:
Do not use a falls risk score as a substitute for a cause.

Scores sort populations. They do not explain this person's Tuesday.

Look at gait, standing blood pressure, medication, vision, feet, floor, bone, and cognition. Then change something that can change.

A high score with no action is documentation, not prevention.

Home-hazard intervention, especially when delivered with occupational therapy and targeted at people already at higher risk, reduces falls.

Grab rails and a tidy trail to the toilet are not interior design. They are treatment.

If the hospital discharge does not mention the home, the discharge is half-finished.
Caption: Home-hazard intervention, especially when delivered with occupational therapy and targeted
Source: Clemson L et al. Cochrane home-hazard review.

Post text:
Standing blood pressure is a two-minute test that still gets skipped.

If your parent falls after standing, after a meal, or after a new blood-pressure tablet, ask for lying and standing measurements.

Dizziness is optional as a symptom. Some people just drop.

Treatable if found. Invisible if not measured.

Vitamin D is important for bone and muscle health. The evidence that it prevents falls as a standalone intervention is not strong enough for NICE to recommend it for that job.

Give vitamin D where deficiency or bone health requires it. Do not pretend a tablet replaces strength and balance training.

Families deserve that distinction. So do services.

A new night sedative is a falls intervention with the wrong sign.

It may buy a quiet night. It also buys unsteadiness at 03:00 on the way to the toilet.

If the presenting problem is nocturnal distress, treat the cause of the distress. Do not add a drug whose main daytime effect is a fall.

Ask what happens at night.

Most falls in homes and in hospitals cluster around the journey to the toilet.

A commode, a light, a clear path, a hearing aid so they hear the instruction, and a review of the water tablet timing: these are not glamorous. They prevent fractures.
Caption: Most falls cluster around the journey to the toilet.

Post text:
Multifactorial programmes can reduce the rate of falls. They do not reliably reduce every fall-related harm in every trial.

That is not an argument for doing nothing. It is an argument for doing the parts with the strongest evidence: exercise, home hazards in high-risk people, medication review, vision.

Collecting risk factors into a form and then changing nothing is the empty version of this intervention.
Source: Hopewell S et al. Br J Sports Med 2020 PMID 33172844.

Post text:
If your parent is 58 and has Parkinson's, a stroke, or a learning disability, falls guidance now includes them, not only people over 65.

Younger high-risk people are easy to miss because they do not look like the poster.

Ask for a falls assessment anyway.
Source: NICE NG249 scope 50+ at higher risk.

Post text:
Delirium and falls share a household.

The person who has fallen may already be delirious. The person who is delirious is about to fall.

Assess both at the front door. A 4AT and a cause-seeking falls history take less time than a later fracture.
Source: Chen 2025 delirium risk factors include prior falls.

Post text:
Fear of falling after the first event is itself a disability.

People stop going out. Muscle goes. The next fall becomes more likely.

A falls service that only talks about rails and not about confidence has missed half the injury.

Ask whether there is a programme, not only a pamphlet.
Caption: Fear of falling after the first event is itself a disability.

Post text:
Feet and footwear are unfashionable and causal.

Long toenails, painful bunions, floppy slippers, and a house that has two steps in the dark will undo an expensive clinic letter.

Look at the feet. Look at the shoes by the door. Write what you see.

If the only outcome of a fall clinic is a pendant alarm, ask what else was considered.

Alarms call help after the event. Exercise, vision, bone treatment and medication review try to prevent the event.

You may need both. You do not need only the alarm.

Do not refer to falls clinic and stop thinking.

The referral letter should say what you have already measured: lying and standing BP, relevant bloods, medication list, bone treatment status, cognitive screen.

A thin letter produces a thin clinic.

A fall that causes a faint or a blackout is syncope until you have thought about it.

Cardiac causes are not common in every cohort, but missing one is costly.

If there is no memory of hitting the ground, or if there is palpitations or exertion in the story, say so clearly on the referral.

Collapse is a different door from a trip.
Caption: Collapse is a different door from a trip.

Post text:
Hospital falls are not always a staffing morality play.

They are also tethers, bed moves, missing glasses, wet floors, night sedation, and a bladder that nobody has assessed.

If your parent falls in hospital, ask what will change tomorrow, not only who will fill in the form tonight.

Care-home falls need the same seriousness as hospital falls, with less equipment around them.

A new faller in a home needs a medical look, not only a mattress on the floor.

Ask the GP to review bone treatment, standing blood pressure and the drug list. Flooring is not a diagnosis.

Strength fades faster than people think when a parent starts sitting through the day.

The intervention is not motivation. It is a programme they can actually attend, or a physiotherapist who will come to the house.

Ask what exists locally. If the answer is nothing, that is a commissioning failure, and you are allowed to say so.

If cognition is impaired, falls prevention still works. It just has to be simpler.

Complexity is how programmes fail people with dementia.
Caption: Complexity is how falls programmes fail people with dementia.

Post text:
Most people who break a hip were never treated for osteoporosis beforehand.

Many are still not treated afterwards.

That is the treatment gap: a fracture that is itself the diagnosis, followed by silence about the bone.

Post text:
They fixed the hip and ignored the bones.

Code the osteoporosis. Treat the osteoporosis. The X-ray has already done the intellectually difficult part.
Caption: The X-ray has already made the diagnosis. Write it down.
Source: US claims analyses: majority of fragility fractures lack an osteoporosis code.

Post text:
Men break bones too. They are even less likely to be offered treatment.

Caption: If your hospital has no Fracture Liaison Service, that is a quality issue.

Undertreatment loves a half-remembered contraindication.

Caption: Dentistry is a planning issue, not a reason to abandon bone treatment.

Post text:
Steroids still steal bone while we treat the other disease.

If you start prednisolone for more than a few weeks in an older person, bone protection is part of the prescription, not an afterthought for clinic two.

Explain it that way.
Caption: The alternative to bone treatment is often another fracture.

Post text:
A hip fracture is never only a bone event.

It is pain, bleeding, immobility, fasting, anaesthesia, constipation, retention, and a high risk of delirium.

Post text:

You are allowed to be interested in the clock.

Caption: After a hip fracture the brain is part of the operation.

Post text:

They are also why bone treatment, nutrition and delirium care are not extras.

If your parent is still wincing when rolled on day two, the pain plan has failed, even if something is written on the chart.

Modified-release oxycodone protocols after hip fracture can over-shoot.

Titrate to the person in front of you. Age, frailty and delirium change the dose the protocol thinks is standard.

People arrive thin, miss meals in fasting windows, and leave thinner.

If the protein sits on the tray and the person is delirious, feeding is a clinical task, not a hospitality extra.

Ask what they have actually swallowed, not what was served.
Caption: Ask what they have swallowed, not what was served.

Post text:
Getting home after a hip fracture depends less on the X-ray and more on whether they can think, stand, eat and toilet.

The implant can be perfect and the person still not be ready.

The implant will not orientate the patient.

Delirium prevention is everybody's decision, not an anaesthesia footnote.

Ask whether bone treatment will start before discharge after a hip fracture.

If the plan is a DXA in four months and a GP letter, many people will fracture again before the appointment.

Caption: Look at the heels. It is part of hip-fracture care.

Post text:
Cognitive assessment belongs in every national hip-fracture registry.

Where delirium and cognition are not measured they are not managed, and hospitals compare their surgery while ignoring the complication that steals independence.

If your registry still treats the brain as optional, change the form.
Source: Merriman / MacLullich Eur Geriatr Med 2025 registries review.

Post text:
If you are a family, you do not need a congress on fragility fracture.

Caption: They will not know who your father was last week unless you tell them.

Post text:
Do not treat postoperative agitation with a blanket ban on analgesia.

Under-treated pain is a standard route into shouting, pulling and then an antipsychotic.

Audit without curiosity is a PDF. Audit with curiosity changes Tuesday.
Caption: Audit with curiosity changes Tuesday.

Post text:
Frailty is not an insult. It is a word for lost reserve.

A small infection, a new tablet, a missed meal, a fall: the same insult that a fitter person shrugs off can take a frail person off their feet and into delirium.

The Clinical Frailty Scale is a conversation about that reserve. It is not a verdict.
Source: Rockwood K et al. CMAJ 2005 CFS PMID 16129869.

Post text:
If your parent has slowed, is more help-dependent, and recovers slowly from ordinary illnesses, you are looking at frailty whether or not anyone has used the word.

The use of the word is that it predicts trouble in hospital and gives you a reason to ask for a geriatric look, a medication review, and a delirium plan.

It is a planning word. Use it.

One describes the last two weeks of reserve. The other detects acute brain failure now.

Using either alone leaves a blind side. Using both is two minutes.

Do not let frail become shorthand for do not bother.

Frail people still benefit from pain treatment, hearing aids, bone drugs, exercise at the right dose, and a search for reversible decline.

Frailty changes the method. It does not cancel the duty.
Caption: Frailty changes the method. It does not cancel the duty.

Post text:
Frailty multiplies the risk of delirium.

High CFS, no delirium plan, is an incomplete clerking.
Source: Chen et al. 2025 frailty OR ~2.05 for delirium.

Post text:
Weight loss, slower walking and needing help with dressing are easier to spot than a score.

If those are new this year, say so at every appointment.

Services still miss frailty when it arrives in ordinary clothes.

Do not assign a CFS from the end of the bed on the day of acute illness.

The score is the baseline of two weeks ago, not the person flattened by pneumonia.

Score the frailty. Then be suspicious of it.

The treatable lookalikes are why geriatric medicine exists.
Caption: Score the frailty. Then be suspicious of it.

Post text:
A good frailty conversation includes what the person still wants.

Not only what they cannot do.

If nobody has asked your parent what a tolerable life looks like, the plan will be generic. Generic plans fail frail people first.

Polypharmacy and frailty travel together.

As people become older and more frail, doses that were reasonable become toxic, especially after an acute injury.

Medication review is not a separate specialty visit. It is part of delirium care and part of frailty care.

A week in bed can take more muscle than a year of ordinary ageing.

If there is no medical reason for the bed, the bed is the problem.

Caption: A single-organ clinic will keep being surprised.
Source: Ellis G et al. Cochrane CGA PMID 28770908.

Post text:

Bring the bag of boxes.

A surprising number of delirium assessments change when the actual night-time tablets are on the desk.
Caption: Bring the bag of boxes.

Post text:

If pain needs an opioid, choose one you can actually titrate.
Caption: If pain needs an opioid, choose one you can actually titrate.

Post text:
Over-the-counter sleep remedies are not harmless because they are on a supermarket shelf.

If the QTc is long, if Lewy body disease is in the story, if the person is merely wandering, look again.

The drug that quiets the bay can also quiet the only person who was trying to tell you they were in pain.
Caption: Haloperidol is not a treatment for delirium. It is sometimes a short-term treatment for da

Post text:
Bladder antimuscarinics treat urgency by blocking acetylcholine.

The bladder is not the only organ that uses acetylcholine.

A medication review after delirium should be a named task, not a hope.

Ask which tablet was stopped, which was reduced, and who will look at the list again in a fortnight.

People go home on the same stack that helped to put them in.
Caption: People go home on the same stack that helped to put them in.

Post text:

Caption: Steroids, opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, some antihistamines, some antidepres

Post text:
If a sleeping tablet was started in hospital, ask whether it is meant to continue at home.

Digoxin, anticonvulsants and some antidepressants become toxic when kidneys or protein binding change in acute illness.

Caption: Ask for the reasoning, not only the stop.

Post text:

Name. What they like to be called. Hearing aids. Glasses. What Monday looked like. Words they use for pain.

Caption: This is new. Please assess for delirium.

Post text:

Today: have they eaten, opened bowels, passed urine, and has anyone checked their thinking.

Four items. Written down. Kindly repeated.

Systems improve when one relative is quietly consistent.

Polite, specific, on the record.

Caption: If the word delirium never appears, ask why not.

Post text:

Ask for the cause list and the review time.

Bring one other relative if you can.

Two listeners hear more of the ward round. One can stay while the other eats.

Caption: A written answer on the table is cheaper than a sedative.

Post text:

That is the whole method.
Caption: You do not need to become a clinician. You need three sentences and a baseline page.

Post text:

A hearing aid in a drawer is a risk factor.

The technology is already in the house. The failure is getting it onto the ear on the day of admission.

Caption: Sometimes medicine does not need a new model. It needs the hearing aid on the ear.

Post text:
A tablet with a familiar face at 21:00 is more useful than a new gadget with a subscription.

Post text:

Liberty versus injury. Record the conversation. Review it.

Caption: The fix is to look at the patient.

Post text:

Match the tool to the actual Tuesday, not to the brochure.

Daylight is technology.

Caption: mRASS serial checks are a way to catch new agitation or new sedation on the ward without w

Post text:

Caption: Treat delirium as a potential brain injury, not a passing fog.

Post text:

Caption: Billions have gone into anti-amyloid drugs that modestly slow decline for some people.

Post text:

Reviewing yesterday's diagnosis as if it were finished is how persistent delirium gets walked past.

A medical diagnosis without the rest of the team is an incomplete treatment.

The tray is a vital sign.
Caption: The tray is a vital sign.

Post text:

Use the whole score, not only the binary delirium cut-point.
Caption: Use the whole 4AT, not only the binary cut-point.

Post text:

Caption: Delirium and pneumonia often arrive as a pair.

Post text:

Caption: Go back into the record and strike the word if it is no longer true.

Post text:

Awareness that lasts one Thursday is not awareness.

Caption: The quiet bed will teach them medicine.

Post text:
Book 1 is a family guide to delirium because leaflets at the bedside arrive too late and say too little.

I am a specialist in one unfashionable condition. The families I meet are specialists in one particular person.

The work is to put those two expertises in the same conversation before the sedation is written up.

That is the whole strategy, on a ward and on here.

If this account is useful, send one post to the sibling who still thinks Mum is just getting old.

Underdiagnosis ends in families before it ends in nations.

One forwarded paragraph is a public-health intervention with no budget.

Twenty thousand followers is not the point.

The point is that the next daughter standing in a bay at 21:00 has the words to say: this is new, please look for delirium, please look for pain, please do not call this old age.

If the account helps that conversation happen earlier, it has done the job. The number will follow.
